children: In a decisive move to rein in stubbornly high inflation, the Federal Reserve on Wednesday unanimously raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point and signaled further tightening ahead as the U.S. economy continues to run hotter than expected.
Here are five key takeaways from the policy decision and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's subsequent press conference.

to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points. Marking the first rate hike in over three years, the move is designed to cool demand and rein in inflation, which has exceeded the Fed's 2% target for more than five years. The unanimous vote underscores a decisive consensus to tighten, a sharp pivot from the three dissenting votes seen in July.

one more 25-basis-point rate hike before the end of 2026. According to the updated Summary of Economic Projections, 12 officials see rates going up once more this year, pushing the median federal funds rate to 4.1% by year-end—up from the 3.8% projected in June. Looking further ahead, the federal funds rate is expected to hold at 4.1% in 2027 before slightly retreating to 3.9% in 2028.

The Fed's longer-run forecast for the benchmark rate has edged up to 3.2%, compared with 3.1% in previous projections, suggesting that policymakers believe the theoretical neutral rate—the interest rate level that neither stimulates nor restricts economic growth—has fundamentally shifted higher.

Alongside the rate hike, the committee adjusted its broader economic outlook. Officials raised their estimates for GDP growth and lowered their forecasts for the unemployment rate. However, inflation projections were also revised upward, underscoring that price pressures remain stubbornly ingrained in the strengthening economy.

forward guidance, opting instead to provide backward guidance on why the Fed hiked today after pausing in July. Noting that underlying inflation is not moving toward the 2% goal at a sufficient speed, Warsh highlighted three main drivers behind the decision:
Economic strength: Recent data proves the broader economy has strengthened.
Stubborn inflation: Longer-term inflation trends simply "weren’t passing the test."
Evolving global hot spots altered the Fed's risk assessments, requiring a removal of monetary accommodation.
